commandments.title: Risk a fixed fraction
commandments.body: Beginners: 0.5–1% of bankroll per idea. Ten losses in a row must still leave a desk.

commandments.title: Trade only after-fee EV
commandments.body: Price is implied probability. Your estimate must beat the market by more than Kalshi’s fee.

commandments.title: Write a number
commandments.body: Not “I think it goes up.” A precise probability you can score later.

commandments.title: Outside view first
commandments.body: Base rates of similar windows, then adjust. Stories come second.

commandments.title: Journal before the outcome
commandments.body: Thesis, probability, size, invalidation, review time — written while you can still be honest.

commandments.title: Process over P&L
commandments.body: A clean stand-down is a win. A lucky bad process is a future blow-up.

commandments.title: Hard loss limits
commandments.body: Daily and weekly caps. Hit them, stop. No revenge windows.

commandments.title: Name the clock
commandments.body: A 15-minute up/down is not a daily structure. Timeframe disagreement is usually a wait.

commandments.title: Hold when you have edge
commandments.body: On binary contracts, selling early often gives the edge back to the book.

commandments.title: Triage ruthlessly
commandments.body: Spend effort only where extra work can produce an edge. Skip easy chalk and opaque chaos.

lessons.title: Paper is the job
lessons.idea: This school is a research desk, not a casino tour.
body: Satoshi’s Council is paper-first. The Classroom is the same. You are training a process that can survive hundreds of windows, not hunting a lucky 15-minute print.

Kalshi event contracts pay $1 if you are right and $0 if you are wrong. The price you pay is the market’s implied probability. That is a research instrument. It is also a way to lose the full stake on a single idea.
Until you can name your edge, your size, and your invalidation without flinching, you do not scale. A well-formed stand-down is a completed decision.
lessons.callout: Patience is a position. A clean WAIT is not a missed trade.
remember: No live size until a sample exists under these rules.
This desk is not Kalshi, and it does not place orders.
You can lose the full stake on a contract.

quiz.q: What is the correct use of this Classroom in week one?

choices.label: Find a 15-minute lock and size it live
Build a written process and paper-track it
Copy SATOSHI’s last call with real money

quiz.why: The product is the method. Live size before process is how desks vanish.

quiz.q: A stand-down with a written reason is…

choices.label: A signal to double the next window

quiz.why: The desk scores process. Sitting when evidence is incomplete is the job.

lessons.title: Bankroll before opinion
lessons.idea: Size is decided before the story is allowed to speak.
body: Pick a Classroom bankroll you can lose without changing family or work. Write it down. All size in this school is a percent of that number, never a feeling.
Beginner risk: 0.5–1% per idea. On a $500 paper book that is $2.50–$5.00. It looks small. That is the point. Twenty losses in a row at 1% still leave most of the book.
On Kalshi, the dollars at risk on a YES bought at 40¢ is the 40¢, not the $1 face. Still cap the notional so a cluster of windows cannot wipe the week.
lessons.callout: If the size needs to be large to feel interesting, the process is already broken.
remember: Risk % is non-negotiable math.
Daily loss limit: 3%. Weekly: 6%. Hit it, stop.
Never add size to a loser to “get even.”

quiz.q: A beginner with a $1,000 paper bankroll should risk about how much on one idea?
quiz.why: 0.5–1% of $1,000 is $5–$10. Survivability first.

quiz.q: You lose two windows. Next action?

choices.label: Keep the same % and log both
Switch to a new market you have not studied

quiz.why: Fixed fraction. The journal does the teaching, not the next bet.

lessons.title: Why Bitcoin exists
lessons.idea: You cannot price Bitcoin if you think it is only a chart.
body: Money is a coordination tool: a way to store work across time. Fiat can be issued. Bitcoin’s supply is capped at 21 million, issued on a known schedule, and settled by a network that does not need a permissioned intermediary.

That does not make every 15-minute candle sacred. It does mean the asset has a monetary policy you can actually describe. Halvings, issuance, and long-term holder behavior are context for higher-timeframe reads.
Trade the window in front of you. Understand the asset so a headline does not become your entire thesis.
lessons.callout: Read The Bitcoin Standard here. The Classroom will not replace it.
remember: Scarcity is a policy, not a slogan.
Volatility is a feature of price discovery, not proof the idea is broken.
ETH on this desk is a signal into BTC, not a second casino.

quiz.q: Bitcoin’s 21 million cap is best understood as…

choices.label: A marketing target that can be voted away next week
A monetary rule enforced by the protocol and the network
A reason every 15-minute window must go up

quiz.why: The cap is protocol. It does not dictate the next candle.

lessons.title: Blocks, nodes, proof of work
lessons.idea: A short technical picture so the tape is not magic.
body: Transactions are grouped into blocks. Miners expend energy to propose the next block (proof of work). Nodes independently check the rules. That is why “don’t trust, verify” is not a poster — it is the architecture.

You do not need to run a miner to trade a Kalshi window. You do need to know that settlement of Bitcoin itself is not the same as settlement of a Kalshi BTC contract. Kalshi settles on a stated index (often a CME reference for daily markets; short windows have their own rules). Read the contract.
Inventing Bitcoin is the companion text: double-spend, timestamps, and why a chain of work solves them.
lessons.callout: Name the settlement source before you name the direction.
remember: Spot Bitcoin and a Kalshi contract are different instruments.
If you cannot find how it settles, you do not trade it.

quiz.q: A Kalshi BTC 15-minute contract settles…

choices.label: When your hardware wallet confirms a transaction
By the market’s written rule / reference for that ticker

quiz.why: Always the contract text. The Council is research, not the exchange.

lessons.title: Keys, custody, hygiene
lessons.idea: Trading skill is worthless if you lose the coins to a phishing page.
body: A private key is control. A seed phrase is the backup of that control. Anyone who sees it owns the coins. Hardware wallets, offline backups, and a refusal to type seeds into websites are the adult version of this lesson.
Kalshi is a CFTC-regulated venue with KYC and fiat rails. That is a different trust model than self-custody. Use it as a venue, not as a wallet for your life savings.
Classroom rule: never mix “I am learning contracts” with “I just moved the family stack.”
lessons.callout: Self-custody for Bitcoin you intend to hold. Venue accounts for research size only.
remember: No seed phrase on screenshots, chats, or cloud notes.
Phishing looks like the real site. Bookmark it.

quiz.q: Your Kalshi login should hold…

choices.label: Only capital you treat as research / risk capital

quiz.why: Venue money is risk capital. Savings do not live there.

lessons.title: The $1 contract
lessons.idea: Price is a probability. Payout is binary.
body: You buy YES if you think the event happens, NO if you think it does not. A contract bought at 0.37 implies the market’s 37% chance. If you are right at settlement, it is worth $1. If you are wrong, it is worth $0.
Example: buy YES at 37¢. Win: +63¢ per contract. Lose: −37¢. Fees come out of that. If you believe the true chance is 55%, you may have edge — after you subtract the fee.
Limit orders let you name the price. Market orders pay the spread. Beginners default to limits unless the book is thick and the window is dying.
lessons.callout: If you cannot write “market says X%, I say Y%,” you do not have a trade.
remember: Implied probability = contract price.
Always compute EV after fees.
Read the exact question, including time and index.

quiz.q: A YES at 70¢ implies the market thinks the event is…
quiz.why: Price is the implied probability, not a multiplier.

quiz.q: You estimate 80% and the YES is 70¢. Before fees this is…

choices.label: Positive EV if you are calibrated

quiz.why: EV ≈ 0.80×0.30 + 0.20×(−0.70) = +0.10 per dollar of face, before fees.

lessons.title: Fees eat thin edges
lessons.idea: A 2-point “edge” can be a fee in disguise.
body: Kalshi’s taker fee is roughly 0.07 × price × (1 − price) per contract. Around 50¢ that is about 1.75¢. Near the wings it shrinks. You still pay on both entry and an early exit.
Never quote edge in your head without the fee. The Lab tab on this Classroom does the arithmetic so you stop guessing.
Thick books and patient limits reduce the hidden tax of crossing the spread. Thin 15-minute books can turn a fair idea into a bad fill.
lessons.callout: If the edge does not survive the fee table, there is no trade.
remember: Compute fee at the actual price, not at 50¢ by habit.
Early exit can double the fee hit.

quiz.q: The most honest way to decide if a Kalshi idea is tradable is…

choices.label: Whether the last three windows paid
Expected value after fees and spread

quiz.why: Fees and spread are part of the price. Ignore them and you are buying noise.

lessons.title: Clocks: 15m, hourly, daily
body: A 15-minute up/down asks whether price finishes above or below a strike by the close of that window. Microstructure, book imbalance, and panic matter more than a halving essay.
Hourly and daily thresholds ask a slower question. Structure, session, and scheduled data (CPI, FOMC) start to matter. Annual brackets are a different sport again.
The Council’s 15-min tab is a lens on the same debate — not a new bot farm. If 1h and 15m disagree, that disagreement is information. It is usually a wait, not a reason to mash both.
lessons.callout: Name the clock before you name the opinion.
remember: Do not import a daily thesis into a 4-minute window.
Near-settled 99¢ chalk is not a skill trade.

quiz.q: When the 15-minute book and the daily structure disagree, the Classroom default is…

choices.label: Trade both to “be in the market”
Stand down or treat them as separate questions

quiz.why: Different clocks. Forcing one story onto both is how people overtrade.

lessons.title: Write a probability
lessons.idea: “Probably” is not a number you can grade.
body: Superforecasters translate hunches into percents, then update in small steps as evidence arrives. They start with the outside view: how often do windows like this resolve up? Then they adjust.
Calibration is a promise to audit. If you say 70% often, about 7 in 10 of those should happen. The Council’s Calibration tab exists because a confidence number that never verifies is decoration.
Keep a personal calibration log in the Journal: stated %, outcome, error. That is how you stop being a hedgehog with one story.
lessons.callout: Read Superforecasting in this track. It is the prediction-market book.
remember: Outside view first, inside view second.
Update often, in small increments, unless the evidence is shocking.
Score yourself. Memory will lie.

quiz.q: The outside view for a 15-minute BTC window starts with…

choices.label: Base rates of similar windows (session, vol, distance to strike)

quiz.why: Tetlock: anchor on the class of events, then adjust.

lessons.title: Expected value is the only ticket
lessons.idea: If EV is not clearly positive after costs, pass.
body: EV = (your p × profit if right) + ((1 − p) × loss if wrong) − fees. Use the Lab. Do not do this in a panic with 40 seconds left.
A 4-point gap at 92¢ is not the same as a 4-point gap at 48¢. Fees, jump risk, and the chance you are miscalibrated all change the quality of the bet.
Kelly is a ceiling, not a target. Half-Kelly or a hard 1% cap — whichever is smaller. Beginners do not full-Kelly a 15-minute coin.
lessons.callout: Pass is a position. Most windows should be passes.
remember: Edge must clear fees and your own error bars.
Do not average into a thesis that failed its invalidation.

quiz.q: You have a 3-point edge at 50¢ after fees, but you are a beginner. Best size?

choices.label: A small fixed fraction, or skip if unsure
The whole bankroll — the math is on your side

quiz.why: Calibration error is the hidden term. Size small until the journal proves you.

lessons.title: Triage: Goldilocks questions
lessons.idea: Do not spend brain on clocks you cannot beat or chaos you cannot model.
body: Tetlock’s first commandment is triage. Easy chalk (99¢ with seconds left) is not where work pays. Opaque “anything can happen” clouds are not either. The middle — where information is public but not fully priced — is the job.
On Kalshi BTC, that often means mid-window books, scheduled data, or a documented disagreement between options, spot, and the contract — not a vibes-based smash of the close.
If you cannot say why the market is wrong in one sentence that a skeptical partner would respect, you do not have triage. You have a hunch.
lessons.callout: Work only where extra effort can move the number.
remember: Skip 99¢ chalk as a “skill” trade.
Skip questions you cannot settle in your own notes.

quiz.q: A 99¢ YES with 20 seconds left is usually…

choices.label: Chalk — not where process work pays

quiz.why: Triage. Easy remaining probability is not a research edge.

lessons.title: Position size from the stop, not the vibe
lessons.idea: On binaries, the “stop” is often hold-to-settle. Size must assume the full loss.
body: Spot traders place a stop and size from the distance to it. Binary contracts often have no graceful stop — early exit can be worse. So assume you lose the premium. Size = (bankroll × risk%) / premium per contract.
Example: $2,000 book, 1% risk = $20. YES at 40¢ → at most 50 contracts, and less after fees. If that feels too small to bother, good. You are not supposed to need drama.
Cluster risk: five 15-minute windows in one hour are not five independent bets if they share the same tape shock. Cap correlated exposure.
lessons.callout: Correlated windows count as one idea in disguise.
remember: Size from max loss, not from hoped-for payout.
One thesis, one risk unit — even if it prints as three tickers.

quiz.q: Four 15-minute BTC windows in the same hour after a CPI print are…
quiz.why: Same shock, same book. Treat the cluster as one unit.

lessons.title: The head is the risk engine
lessons.idea: Trading in the Zone exists because willpower does not.
body: Revenge trading, FOMO, and moving a rule after a loss are not personality quirks. They are the default. Professionals install hard brakes: cooldown after a loss, daily cap, no adding to a loser, no new markets after two consecutive misses.
Douglas’s point: the next window is independent of your last P&L. Your process is not. If you broke a rule, the review is about the rule, not the candle.
Classroom drill: after any loss, walk away for one full window. Log emotion 1–10. If it is above 6, you are done for the session.
lessons.callout: Protect mental capital the same way you protect dollars.
remember: One loss → mandatory cooldown.
Never widen a thesis after it is invalidated.
Read Trading in the Zone in this track.

quiz.q: You just lost. The Classroom rule is…

choices.label: Cooldown of at least one window and a journal line
Increase size because the setup is “due”

quiz.why: Brakes are designed, not felt.

lessons.title: The journal is the school
lessons.idea: If it is not written before the outcome, it did not happen.
body: Required fields: market, thesis, your probability, market price, size, invalidation, review time. Optional: emotion, which commandment you used.
After settlement: outcome, process score (0–5), one sentence on whether you followed the rules. A profitable broken rule scores worse than a losing clean pass.
Weekly: count stand-downs, rule breaks, and calibration error. That weekly review is how this scales from beginner to a desk.
lessons.callout: Write it before the market can flatter or embarrass you.
remember: Use the Journal tab on every paper idea.
Process score is independent of P&L.

quiz.q: A winning trade taken after the invalidation fired is scored as…

choices.label: A process miss that got lucky
Proof the invalidation was wrong forever

quiz.why: Luck is not a method.

lessons.title: Confluence, not applause
lessons.idea: Four copies of one idea are still one idea.
body: On the Round Table, SATOSHI locks a directional call only with confluence — at least 3 of 4 advisors — and no veto from RAIJIN or ORACLE. That is not theatre. Independent lanes (structure, momentum, crowding, process health) must agree for a reason.
Your personal version: do not count Twitter, a friend, and a lagging RSI as three votes. Count independent evidence. A dissent you cannot answer is a wait.
Advisors on the Council are ranked by record, not title. You should rank your own tools the same way. A hot streak of three is not a 40-of-55.
lessons.callout: Satoshi locks only when the table earns it.
remember: Independent lanes > duplicate signals.
A veto (crowding, bad data, broken process) forces stand-down.

quiz.q: Three indicators that all read the same 5-minute momentum are…
quiz.why: Confluence requires different kinds of evidence.

lessons.title: WAIT is a position
lessons.idea: Incomplete evidence is not a dare.
body: The Council records why it sits and when it will look again. You will too. “No aligned evidence” is a complete sentence.
Boredom, a quiet Sunday, or a need to “use” the bankroll are not theses. They are how people donate the fee table.
A WAIT that later would have lost is a process win. Track those. They are the hidden P&L of a grown desk.
lessons.callout: No aligned evidence means no active thesis.
remember: Write the next review time on every WAIT.
Do not fill dead air with size.

quiz.q: The correct next step after a documented WAIT is…

choices.label: Force a small trade so the hour “counts”
Review at the time you wrote, with the same rules
Delete the note so it does not look idle

quiz.why: A WAIT without a review time is just avoidance.

lessons.title: The 15-minute lens
lessons.idea: Same council, faster clock — still paper.
body: Short Kalshi BTC windows are often dominated by order-book imbalance, panic fades, and cross-asset bleed (ETH/SOL lagging a BTC spike by seconds). Macro essays rarely beat that clock.

Rules that survive this lens: high-conviction only, 2% of bankroll max (1% while learning), hold to settle when the edge is real, one idea per window. Do not sell a good number because the last thirty seconds feel loud.
If the Council is at stand-down, you do not freelance a 15-minute hero trade “because it is small.” Small and frequent is how bankrolls die.
lessons.callout: The 15-min tab is a lens, not a license.
remember: Microstructure > manifesto on this clock.
One trade at a time per window.
Paper until the journal is boringly good.

quiz.q: SATOSHI is at stand-down and a 15-minute book looks “easy.” You…

choices.label: Respect the stand-down unless your written process independently earns a pass
Copy the loudest seat on the floor

quiz.why: The lens does not override confluence and veto. Freelance is not a method.

lessons.title: How this scales
lessons.idea: A school that cannot grow is a pamphlet.
body: Path: finish the oath, then Bitcoin, then Kalshi, then edge math, then risk, then desk. Do not skip to 15-minute tactics.
Promotion rule (personal): 50 journaled ideas, process score ≥ 4 on 80% of them, calibration error shrinking — then consider a slightly larger fraction, still capped.
The method travels: evidence, dissent, decision, review. That is the Council Method for a market window or a leadership call. The Classroom is how you install it in your hands.
lessons.callout: Scale process first. Size is a consequence.
remember: No size increase without a sample.
Keep the commandments visible.
Return to lessons when a rule breaks — not to a hotter chart.

quiz.q: You want to raise size. The Classroom requires…

choices.label: A documented sample and clean process scores

quiz.why: Size follows evidence of process, not a hot streak.
